summary:
Legal gender recognition in Taiwan remains gated by a 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery before a gender marker can be changed on the national ID. An estimated 90% of trans people are blocked from obtaining a document that matches their presentation, which turns every ID-requiring interaction, including clinic visits and airport security checks, into a potential site of distress and discrimination. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013, but the surgical requirement stands.

In August 2024 a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change her ID marker without surgery or a psychological evaluation; the rights group supporting her indicated an appeal was likely. No tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction access occurred during 2025.

Private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and gender characteristics in education under the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, with a NT$100,000 fine for schools that discriminate in admission, instruction or assessment; sexual-bullying prevention and reporting duties were added in June 2011. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since the 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment, with fines of NT$300,000 to NT$1,500,000. The Long-Term Care Services Act of January 2017 carries an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 of 24 May 2017 held that the Constitution's Article 7 discrimination grounds are illustrative rather than exhaustive, extending the right to equality to sexual orientation.

Public facilities are a documented pressure point. The Ministry of Environment is spending NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms from 623 to 1,246 by 2029, and an LGBTQ+ rights group found that only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage. Among trans and gender-nonconforming survey respondents who reported discrimination, 17% of the incidents occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms.

For a trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship, partner recognition is partial. Same-sex couples can legally adopt: since May 2023 legislation has granted full adoption rights, replacing the stepchild-only rights in place since 2019, and a January 2022 court order had already allowed one couple to adopt before the legislature codified full rights. Single individuals, including individual LGBT people, may adopt depending on circumstances. The Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, excluding both single women and couples the law reads as same-sex.

Conversion therapy is effectively banned under a Ministry of Health and Welfare letter of 22 February 2018, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.

Political hostility to trans rights has grown. Organisations in the anti-gender movement have aligned with anti-trans policies promoted abroad, and the Taiwan Solidarity Party has called for a 'two genders' position. The seventh annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei drew an estimated 3,000 people in November 2025 despite rain, with international participants, and called for an end to discrimination against trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Taiwan's criminal-law trajectory on same-sex conduct is historical: a 1740 Qing decree criminalised voluntary homosexual intercourse between adults, punishable by a month in prison and 100 heavy blows; the Republic of China's provisional criminal code abolished explicit prohibitions on 'consenting ji jian' around 1912; and sodomy was decriminalised when the ROC took over Taiwan after World War II under the 1935 criminal code. During martial law, LGBT people were harassed and detained under general public order laws, the Temporary Provisions against the Communist Rebellion, repealed in 1991.

Public expression has expanded over two decades. The first Taiwan Pride was held in Taipei on 1 November 2003 with over 1,000 attendees, growing to about 80,000 by 2015, 137,000 in 2018 and 170,000 by 2019, with pride events also held in Kaohsiung since 2010 and Taichung drawing 20,000 in 2016. In 2022 Taiwan withdrew from hosting WorldPride 2025 over the disputed name 'WorldPride Kaohsiung', which the public and government considered offensive, and the event moved to Washington, D.C. in June 2025.

The current anti-gender mobilisation follows earlier political flashpoints over school curricula. In November 2018 voters passed a referendum question banning LGBT-inclusive sex education (Question 11) and rejected the pro-inclusion Question 15; Education Minister Yeh Jiunn-rong said LGBT content would be reviewed against the result, and an earlier Ministry of Education curriculum reform announced in March 2010 and effective in 2011 had already been watered down to 'respecting diverse sexual orientations' after anti-LGBT opposition.
localsOnly:
Pending changes to conscription criteria could actively harm trans people in Taiwan, and the government recorded no tangible policy movement on the surgery requirement or assisted reproduction during 2025.

Following the November 2018 referendum, suicide hotlines reported a 40% surge in calls from LGBT individuals, particularly adolescents and young adults.

Conversion therapy is effectively banned by a Ministry of Health and Welfare letter of 22 February 2018, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.
outOfScopeNotes:
The legalclarity.org page on Taiwan's transgender rights, laws and gaps was unavailable at research time (HTTP 404, page removed), so its content is not reflected here.

Whether the 2008 executive order requiring surgery has been amended since the August 2024 Taipei court ruling is unresolved in the sources. The outcome of the appeal indicated in that case is not sourced. The number of trans people who have obtained a gender-marker change is not sourced, so the 90% figure rests on the cited estimate rather than a registry count. The content and timing of the pending conscription-criteria changes are not sourced beyond their being pending.
